verses.text: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth.

He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them,
and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.
He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and persuaded Jews and Greeks.
But when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.
When they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!”
He departed there, and went into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent;
for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you;
but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.”
So he drove them from the judgment seat.
Then all the Greeks laid hold on Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.
Paul, having stayed after this many more days, took his leave of the brothers,  and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow.
He came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself entered into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay with them a longer time, he declined;
but taking his leave of them, and saying, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills,” he set sail from Ephesus.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch.
Having spent some time there, he departed, and went through the region of Galatia, and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.
Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him, and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace;
for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.

footnotes.content: Paul leaves the philosophers behind in Athens and heads to Corinth—a busy, pagan port city. Sometimes the Lord's work isn't in the halls of learning but in the streets and workshops where ordinary people toil. Notice he doesn't give up; he just changes his route.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here we meet Aquila and Priscilla—exiled from Rome by Claudius's decree against the Jews. Paul finds them, and they become inseparable companions in his work. Sometimes the Lord weaves broken lives together into something beautiful and purposeful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul works at tentmaking with his hands—the apostle doesn't live above the people he serves. There's a humility here, a willingness to labor beside others. The gospel never came dressed in silk; it came with calloused hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every Sabbath, Paul stands in the synagogue and reasons with Jews and Greeks alike. He's patient, persistent, not afraid to speak to both crowds and hold conversation. The work of faith is often quieter and longer than we'd like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Silas and Timothy arrive, they bring news from other churches—and Paul feels the Spirit surge within him. Suddenly his witness sharpens; he can't help but press harder into the truth about Jesus. That's what fellowship does—it strengthens conviction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they attack him, Paul shakes out his garment in a sign of separation—a hard gesture, but clear. He's not rejecting them cruelly; he's been rejected and now draws a line. Sometimes faithfulness means knowing when to step away and let others face what they've chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Justus's house stands next to the synagogue—how close, and how far! Those who worship God but haven't yet seen Jesus become Paul's neighbors and hosts. Grace often lives in the margins, just outside the old walls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Crispus, the synagogue leader, believes with his whole household. Then many Corinthians follow. When the doors open, they open wide—and faith runs through families like a vine. That's what we pray for: entire households turning to Jesus together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks to Paul in a night vision: "Don't be afraid." How often does the Master speak to us when we're alone, in the darkness, wrestling with doubt? He knows. He comes. He commands us to speak and not fall silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am with you." Such a simple promise, and such an infinite one. No one will harm Paul beyond what the Lord permits—not because life will be easy, but because he won't face it alone. We hear the same word today.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eighteen months. Paul stays put, teaching the word day after day in Corinth—a place so broken, so pagan, so lost. That's patience. That's how God works often: slow, steady, word upon word, life touching life until roots run deep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Gallio arrives as proconsul, Paul's opponents see their chance and drag him before the judgment seat. They move as one, united in their anger. But notice—the Lord has not left His servant undefended. Watch what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They accuse Paul of persuading men to worship God "contrary to the law." But whose law? That's the question underneath. The gospel will always seem dangerous to those who fear truth more than falsehood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gallio, the Roman proconsul, hears the case and sees no crime of real harm in it. Providence works here—a pagan official, following Roman law, becomes an unlikely shield for the gospel. God wastes no instruments; even Gallio serves His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "These are questions about words and names and your own law," Gallio says, declining to judge. He speaks a truth deeper than he knows: the gospel is not a legal matter but a heart matter. No court can settle who Jesus is—only faith can.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gallio sends them away from the judgment seat. Imagine Paul's relief—not condemned, but released. Sometimes the Lord defends us through the indifference of officials who simply have other business.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In their frustration, the Greeks beat Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and Gallio watches without caring. The powerful turn on their own. But here's the mercy: Sosthenes may yet become a believer—we'll see his name again, standing beside Paul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After many days more, Paul sails with Priscilla and Aquila toward Syria. He shaves his head at Cenchreae because of a vow—whether a Nazarite vow or another, we don't know. But his actions show a man still rooted in Jewish faith, even as he moves out into the wider world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephesus welcomes Paul, and he goes straight to the synagogue to reason with the Jews. He never rests from speaking, never grows tired of that conversation. This is his passion: to help people see Jesus in the Scriptures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Ephesians ask him to stay longer, but he declines. Even when people want him, even when the door is open, Paul knows his other duties. Not every "yes" is the Lord's will; sometimes obedience means a loving refusal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I must keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return if God wills," Paul says. See the humility? He doesn't promise; he leaves it with the Lord. And notice how he speaks: not "when I return" but "if God wills." That's a pilgrim's faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul lands at Caesarea, greets the church, and heads south to Antioch. These quick glimpses of travel and fellowship tell us how deeply Paul is connected to the wider body—Jerusalem, Antioch, Asia, Greece. He's woven the churches together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul journeys through Galatia and Phrygia, establishing the disciples. He does the same work Luke recorded before—visiting, strengthening, teaching. The third missionary journey begins in steady, unglamorous faithfulness: one town, one church, one conversation at a time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here comes Apollos—from Alexandria, eloquent, mighty in the Scriptures. Luke introduces him carefully: a man of gifts and learning, fervent with the things of God. But gifts without the full truth need refining. Even Apollos has more to learn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Apollos knows the baptism of John and speaks accurately about Jesus—but only what he knows. His fervent spirit is real; his knowledge is genuine as far as it goes. But it doesn't go far enough. None of us ever finishes learning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Priscilla and Aquila hear him and take him aside to explain "the way of God more accurately." See the gentleness here? No public correction, no shame—just a couple who've walked further inviting a gifted man into deeper truth. That's how the body teaches one another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers encourage Apollos to go to Achaia and write ahead commending him. He arrives and "greatly helps those who had believed through grace." Notice: grace is what lets them believe. All our words and eloquence serve that one reality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Apollos powerfully refutes the Jews from the Scriptures, showing that Jesus is the Christ. Looking back from our time, readers today hear an echo of that same argument—how the Old Testament bears witness to Jesus. We still make that case, still open those same scrolls, grateful that what he refuted then, we affirm now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
